notes:
I've put together notes for most verses of Jeremiah 36. I could only do five searches, and some pages wouldn't load fully, so the coverage has limits:

- **Coverage:** Almost everything comes from enduringword.com (Guzik) and from older commentaries collected on studylight.org, biblehub.com and blueletterbible.org. There is nothing from preceptaustin.org.
- **Tradition differences:** Where traditions differ (v. 3, v. 30), the views come from each tradition's older writers as gathered on those sites. I found nothing on the denominations' own websites.
- **Missing views:** I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, the Orthodox sites, or the prosperity or hyper-grace teachers, so those are left out.
- **Skipped verses:** I had no specific material on v. 13, 15 or 18 beyond what the text itself says.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik places this at or near Babylon's first invasion (605 BC), when Daniel was taken captive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 2:**
- Ellicott thinks Jeremiah could remember the substance of 23 years of preaching. He may also have had earlier written records, sometimes adjusting the wording for new circumstances. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-2.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch say "all the words" shouldn't be taken too strictly, since v. 32 shows more was added later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-2.htm
- Hitzig thought Jeremiah was gathering scattered earlier notes into one book, not writing everything from memory for the first time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-3.htm
- Gill reports a rabbinic tradition (via Kimchi) that this scroll was the book of Lamentations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-2.htm
- Kingcomments says the scroll covered about 23 years, from Josiah's 13th year to Jehoiakim's 4th. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-36.html
- Thompson says a scroll would keep the message alive if the prophet died or society collapsed. He points to the Law scroll found in the temple in 621 BC as a precedent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 3 (where traditions differ: the word "perhaps"):**
- *Shared reading:* Ryken says Jeremiah's warnings of judgment were meant to save people, not just frighten them. Clarke says judgment could still be avoided if the people heard and turned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- *Reformed (Calvin):* "Perhaps" expresses doubt because the people had been stubborn for so long. God speaks in human terms here, since He doesn't actually deliberate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-3.html
- *Matthew Henry (Puritan):* God's foreknowledge had no uncertainty; He knew they would be unfaithful. He used this means anyway, and if it failed they had even less excuse. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-3.html
- *Gill (Calvinist Baptist):* God's purpose to bring judgment would not change, and He knew they wouldn't listen. The method was "humanly speaking" a likely one, and it left them without excuse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-3.htm
- *Methodist (Benson and Thomas Coke):* Benson says God speaks "after the manner of men." Both say expressions like this show that God's foreknowledge doesn't override human free will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-3.htm and https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-3.html
- *Catholic (Haydock):* The word "if" shows free will. Hearing many prophecies together was meant to make a deeper impression. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-3.html
- *Forgiveness:* Benson and Poole say "forgive" could mean both escaping eternal death and being spared earthly punishment, though the earthly one is mainly meant here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-3.htm

**v. 4:**
- Matthew Henry suggests Jeremiah couldn't write as fast or as neatly as Baruch, so he used him as a secretary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-36.html
- Guzik says the prophet didn't have to write the words himself for them to be God's word. Trapp compares Baruch to Tertius writing for Paul (Romans 16:22). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 5 ("restricted"):**
- *Not under arrest:* Harrison says the Hebrew word can mean arrest, but v. 19 shows Jeremiah was free to hide. Cundall thinks he was barred from the temple after his Temple Sermon, though the word could also mean ritual uncleanness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- *A different view:* Chuck Smith takes it as being in prison. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/smith_chuck/c2000_jer/jer_036.cfm
- *Application:* Morgan compares this to Paul writing letters from prison. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 6:** Feinberg notes that before the exile, fasts were called in emergencies rather than on fixed dates. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 7:** Matthew Henry notes a shift from v. 3: God said "perhaps they will hear," and Jeremiah adds "perhaps they will pray." His point is that people need to pray for grace in order to turn. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_036.cfm

**v. 8:** Guzik observes that Baruch obeyed, but no response from the people is recorded. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 9:**
- Harrison dates the fast to December 604 BC and thinks Babylon's capture of Ashkelon probably prompted it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- Feinberg notes that the people, not the king, called the fast. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- Guzik says it's unclear whether this is the same reading as v. 8 or a second one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 10:** Harrison links Gemariah's father Shaphan to Josiah's secretary of state (2 Kings 22). That would possibly make Gemariah the brother of Ahikam, who protected Jeremiah. Ryken calls Shaphan's sons "forgotten heroes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 11:** Matthew Henry's lesson is that when a message helps us, we should pass it on to others. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_036.cfm

**v. 12:** Constable notes that Elnathan son of Achbor had earlier brought the prophet Uriah back from Egypt (Jer. 26). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-36.html

**v. 14:** Thompson thinks the officials' politeness to Baruch shows they were friendly, or perhaps that Baruch was of noble birth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 16:**
- Trapp says the officials didn't dare keep this from the king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- Matthew Henry contrasts their fear here with v. 24, where "so soon" good impressions fade. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_036.cfm

**v. 17:** Kidner praises the officials for checking carefully that the scroll was genuine before acting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 19:**
- Guzik ties this to Uriah's murder (Jer. 26:23): without hiding, Jeremiah and Baruch would likely have been killed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- Harrison mentions a Jewish tradition that they hid in the "Grotto of Jeremiah" outside the Damascus Gate, though how accurate this is remains uncertain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 20–21:** Guzik thinks the officials stored the scroll away to protect it because they expected the king to react badly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 23:**
- Constable says a scroll's columns were called "doors" in Hebrew. He reads the burning as a symbolic claim that the prophecies would end just as the scroll did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-36.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the cutting was repeated, but probably not section by section as each was read. It also says the fire was a portable brazier, not a fixed hearth. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/36-23.htm
- Kidner says the slow, deliberate burning was a stronger rejection than a sudden outburst would have been. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- Guzik sees fear as well as contempt: the king tried to destroy the word because he couldn't simply ignore it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- Guzik also applies Meyer's warning about using a "penknife" on Scripture: skipping, explaining away or doubting the parts we dislike. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 24:** Constable sets this beside Josiah, who tore his clothes when the Law was read (2 Kings 22:11); Jehoiakim tore the scroll instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-36.html

**v. 25:** Constable notes three officials pleaded with the king but couldn't stop him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-36.html

**v. 26:** Keil and Delitzsch say "son of the king" means a royal prince, not Jehoiakim's own son. They read "the LORD hid them" as God graciously keeping them out of sight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-28.htm

**v. 27–28:**
- Gill compares this to the replaced tablets of the Law. The same Spirit brought the prophecies back to Jeremiah's mind, so the burning "signified nothing." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-28.html
- Calvin says not a syllable was to be left out, and the king foolishly thought fire could cut off God's power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-28.html
- The Geneva Bible notes say God raises His word up again and increases it, to the condemnation of those who burn it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-28.htm

**v. 29:**
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers "concerning Jehoiakim" (not "to him"), since contact between king and prophet had broken off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-29.htm
- The Cambridge Bible calls the king's question a loose quotation of Jer. 25:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-29.htm
- Gill says the king spoke as if he cared only about the nation, saying nothing of himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-29.htm

**v. 30 (Jehoiachin did reign; also how this affects the promise to David):**
- *The usual answer:* Jehoiachin's three-month reign "counted as nothing." This is the view of JFB, Poole, the Geneva notes and Barnes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-30.htm
- *Gill:* Nebuchadnezzar never confirmed Jehoiachin as king. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/jeremiah/36-30.html
- *Constable:* Jehoiachin took the throne without authorization. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-30.html
- *Coffman:* Being deposed so quickly fulfilled the prophecy well enough. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-30.html
- *Reformed (Calvin):* Zedekiah wasn't a legitimate successor either, because he was Jehoiakim's brother (the son's uncle). This was a break in David's line, not an end to it; one from Jesse's root, Christ, would come later. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/36-30.html
- *Guzik:* Combined with Jer. 22:30, this curse meant no blood descendant through Jehoiakim could be Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- *Bible Hub article:* Jesus' physical line runs through Nathan (Luke 3), and his legal right comes through Joseph (Matthew 1). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_no_heir_for_Jehoiakim_on_throne.htm
- *Burial:* Poole says the Bible never records how Jehoiakim died. Guzik notes this fulfillment isn't recorded in history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-30.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/
- *Wordplay:* Constable notes a pun in the Hebrew: the king who threw the scroll into the fire would himself be thrown out into the weather. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-36.html

**v. 31:** Benson says the king's family and servants would be punished for their own sins, not his; their link to him only brought it sooner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/36-30.htm

**v. 32:**
- JFB says sinners gain nothing but more punishment by setting God's word aside. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_036.cfm
- Matthew Henry compares the new scroll to a Phoenix rising from the ashes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_036.cfm
- Constable thinks the second scroll probably became the "first draft" of our book of Jeremiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-36.html
- Kingcomments suggests the added words include this chapter's judgment on Jehoiakim. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-36.html
